introduction.text:
**Porta San Giovanni** is a single‑arch gate in Rome’s Aurelian Wall, situated just outside the Archbasilica of Saint John Lateran. Built for **Pope Gregory XIII** in 1574, the gate was designed by the architect **Giacomo della Porta**—though some sources credit **Giacomo del Duca**, who had worked with Michelangelo on Porta Pia.

The structure is more reminiscent of a villa entrance than a defensive work: it lacks side towers, ramparts, and battlements, and is marked by pronounced rustication and a large bearded head that crowns the arch on its external face.

Above the arch a commemorative inscription records the pope’s patronage and the year of construction. The gate opens onto Via Campana (today Via Appia Nuova), a road that for its first three miles follows the ancient Via Asinaria and then the Via Labicana, and whose name reflects both its destination in Campania and the surrounding Roman Campagna.

In addition to its architectural significance, the gate has long been associated with the now‑forgotten **Notte di San Giovanni** festival, in which Romans once celebrated on 23 June with fireworks, rattles, and the symbolic eating of slugs to reconcile disputes.

The modern Appio‑Latino quarter, created in 1926 by demolishing surrounding houses and vineyards, and the fornici (traffic lanes) opened at the gate’s sides that same year, remain visible today.

history.description: Its opening led to the definitive closure of the neighbouring Porta Asinaria, an older Aurelian gate that had become unusable by the 1570s due to rising road levels.
The gate was inaugurated in 1574 as part of Pope Gregory XIII’s reorganisation of the Lateran area to accommodate increased traffic to and from southern Italy.
In 1926 the modern Appio‑Latino quarter was created by demolishing surrounding houses, vineyards, and inns, and fornici were opened at the gate’s sides to improve traffic flow.
The gate was built to facilitate traffic to and from southern Italy, reflecting the broader reorganisation of the Lateran area.
The gate is linked to the now‑forgotten Notte di San Giovanni festival, where Romans once celebrated with fireworks and the symbolic eating of slugs to reconcile disputes.

design.description: The gate is a single grand arch that resembles a villa entrance rather than a defensive structure; it lacks side towers, ramparts, and battlements, and features pronounced rustication.
A large bearded head crowns the arch on its external side, serving as the main decorative element.
Above the arch a Latin inscription commemorates Pope Gregory XIII’s patronage and the year of construction.

art.description: The bearded head sculpture on the arch’s external face is a notable artistic feature of the gate.
The Latin inscription above the arch is also considered an artistic element, combining text and stonework.
